query: How should interaction terms (e.g., innovation × environmental challenge) be centered and standardized to minimize multicollinearity and aid interpretation?

response.query: How should interaction terms (e.g., innovation × environmental challenge) be centered and standardized to minimize multicollinearity and aid interpretation?
response.answer: Center interaction terms by subtracting the mean of each variable involved. Do not standardize interaction terms; instead, standardize the original variables before creating interaction terms. This minimizes multicollinearity and aids interpretation.

#### Stack Exchange Network. I also have interaction terms (in some specifications, even fourth-order terms). As far as I know, multicollinearity can be safely ignored as regards interaction terms. If this is correct, should I test multicollinearity without taking into consideration interaction terms? If it is not correct, should I standardized continuous variables used to generate interaction terms? ## 1 Answer 1. The very idea of testing for multicollinearity is dubious or even plain wrong, see Dave Giles blog post. However, you may still be interested in the level of multicollinearity observed in your sample for diagnostic purposes. Should you include interaction terms in testing for multicollinearity? I would include all regressors regardless of whether they are original variables or were generated as interactions of original variables. I would do that because the effect of multicollinearity will be the same regardless of the interpretation of the particular regressors (variables' names and interpretations do not matter when multiplying or inverting matrices). Will standardizing the variables help avoid multicollinearity? I doubt that standardizing variables (subtracting estimated mean and dividing by estimated standard deviation) will help. If two variables $y$ and $x$ are perfectly collinear, that means. If you define standardized variables $\tilde{y}=\frac{y-\bar{y}}{\hat \sigma\_y}$ and $\tilde{x}=\frac{x-\bar{x}}{\hat \sigma\_x}$, the linear relationship between the standardized variables will still hold:. and hence the multicollinearity will still be there. The same logic applies also for imperfect multicollinearity where equality is approximate rather than strict. However, see Remedies for multicollinearity point 6. ## Your Answer. Title: multicollinearity - Interaction term using centered variables hierarchical regression analysis? What variables should we center? - Cross Validated
#### Stack Exchange Network. Stack Exchange network consists of 183 Q&A communities including Stack Overflow, the largest, most trusted online community for developers to learn, share their knowledge, and build their careers. ### your communities. ### more stack exchange communities. Stack Overflow for Teams is now called **Stack Internal**. Bring the best of human thought and AI automation together at your work. # Interaction term using centered variables hierarchical regression analysis? What variables should we center? Do we calculate the interaction term using the centered variables? Do we have to center ALL the continuous variables we have in the dataset, except the dependent variable? When we have to log some variables (because their s.d. is way higher than their mean), do we then center the variable that has just been logged or the initial one? For example: Variable "Turnover" ---> Logged Turnover (because the s.d. is too high compared to the mean) ---> Centered\_Turnover? OR would it be directly Turnover --> Centered\_Turnover (and we work with this one). You should center the terms involved in the interaction to reduce collinearity e.g. x1 <- rnorm(1000, 10, 1). y <- x1 + rnorm(1000, 5, 5) + x2*rnorm(1000) + x1*x2*rnorm(1000). m1 <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x1*x2). m2 <- lm(y ~ x1cent + x2cent + x1cent*x2cent). lm(formula = y ~ x1 + x2 + x1 * x2). x1:x2 1.179 3.375 0.349 0.727. F-statistic: 0.7865 on 3 and 996 DF, p-value: 0.5015. lm(formula = y ~ x1cent + x2cent + x1cent * x2cent). x1cent -4.106 3.186 -1.289 0.198. x1cent:x2cent 1.179 3.375 0.349 0.727. codes: 0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1. Whether you center other variables is up to you; centering (as opposed to standardizing) a variable that is not involved in an interaction will change the meaning of the intercept, but not other things e.g. y <- x1 + rnorm(1000, 5, 5). But you should take logs of variables because it makes sense to do so or because the residuals from the model indicate that you should, not because they have a lot of variability. results.title: Adding Interaction Terms to Multiple Linear Regression, how to standardize? - Cross Validated
results.content: # Adding Interaction Terms to Multiple Linear Regression, how to standardize? 2. Multiply corresponding standardized values from specific variables to create the interaction terms and then add these new variables to the set of regression data. Should I standardize the interaction term variables also after calculating the 'raw' terms? The standardized interaction term should be the standardized version of the product of the two original variables, **not** the product of the two standardized variables. However, if we use the product of the standardized variables, the results will different than the original. So, if I follow your advice correctly, you're saying that I should first find the product of raw variables and then standardize the new interaction variable for use in the regression? Both ways give the same model, as indicated by the identical ANOVA results, but the interpretation of mpg and weight variable will differ. * $\begingroup$ Correct me if I'm wrong, but are you basically saying that it is wrong to calculate an interaction term by multiplying standardized or centered values? Mean-centering (a part of standardization) makes the lower order terms more interpretable. Note that this is a consequence of the change in interpretation of lower order terms when you mean-center variables before forming the interaction term. In short, when you mean-center/standardize before forming your interaction terms, the mpg effect is the effect of mpg when for an average weight car (because it is the effect when all other variables it interacts with is 0, and for the weight variables we set 0 to equal the mean). For continuous variables, you only need to multiply two variables to form an interaction (again after mean-centering or standardizing if you wish). Knowing that all of the variables are continuous, would you suggest standardizing all variables, calculating interaction terms using standardized values, and then running the regression without standardizing the interaction terms? 6") Standardize binary variable to create interaction term in regression? Correct way to standardize interaction term with one binary and one continuous variable? 1") can i compute an interaction variable by multiplying a standardized variable and a mean centered variable?
